entities.name: Phishing campaigns
entities.evidence: Phishing campaigns as a primary method for stealing victim credentials [T1566].

entities.name: Exploitation of unpatched software vulnerabilities
entities.evidence: Exploitation of unpatched software vulnerabilities [T1190] through Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) such as:

entities.name: CVE-2024-1709
entities.evidence: ScreenConnect vulnerability CVE-2024-1709 [CWE-288: Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel].

entities.name: CVE-2023-48788
entities.evidence: Fortinet EMS SQL injection vulnerability CVE-2023-48788 [CWE 89: SQL Injection].

entities.name: CVE-2025-10035
entities.evidence: Fortra GoAnywhere vulnerability CVE-2025-10035 [CWE-502: Deserialization of Untrusted Data].

entities.name: CVE-2026-1731
entities.evidence: BeyondTrust vulnerability CVE-2026-1731 [CWE-78: OS Command Injection].

entities.name: Living off the land (LOTL) techniques
entities.evidence: Medusa actors use living off the land (LOTL) techniques and legitimate tools, such as Advanced IP Scanner and SoftPerfect Network Scanner for initial user, system, and network enumeration.

entities.name: PowerShell
entities.evidence: Medusa actors use PowerShell [T1059.001] and the Windows Command Prompt (cmd.exe) [T1059.003] for network [T1046] and filesystem enumeration [T1083] and to utilize Ingress Tool Transfer capabilities [T1105].

entities.name: Ingress Tool Transfer

entities.name: Certutil
entities.evidence: Certutil (certutil.exe), an administrator utility used to manage public key infrastructure (PKI) and download files, is used to avoid detection when performing file ingress.

entities.name: Minidump (comsvcs.dll)
entities.evidence: Medusa actors also use Minidump (comsvcs.dll) to avoid detection when dumping Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) credentials.

relationships.evidence: Medusa actors typically recruit initial access brokers (IABs) in cybercriminal forums and marketplaces to obtain initial access to potential victims.
Medusa actors use a double-extortion model where they encrypt victim data and threaten to publicly release exfiltrated data if a ransom is not paid.
Medusa actors use living off the land (LOTL) techniques and legitimate tools, such as Advanced IP Scanner and SoftPerfect Network Scanner for initial user, system, and network enumeration.

Medusa actors use PowerShell [T1059.001] and the Windows Command Prompt (cmd.exe) [T1059.003] for network [T1046] and filesystem enumeration [T1083] and to utilize Ingress Tool Transfer capabilities [T1105].
Medusa actors use Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) [T1047] for querying system information.
Medusa actors exploit legitimate tools and use LOTL techniques to avoid detection.
Certutil (certutil.exe), an administrator utility used to manage public key infrastructure (PKI) and download files, is used to avoid detection when performing file ingress.
Medusa actors use several different PowerShell stealth techniques with increasing complexity; these are provided below.
Medusa actors attempt to cover their tracks by deleting the PowerShell command line history [T1070.003].
In this example, Medusa actors use a well-known stealth technique that executes a base64 encrypted command [T1027.013] using specific execution settings.
In another example, the DownloadFile string is obfuscated by slicing it into pieces and referencing it via a variable [T1027].

In the bind shell, the script awaits a connection on local port 443 [T1071.001] and initiates a connection to a remote port 443 in the reverse shell.
Medusa actors attempted to use vulnerable or signed drivers to kill or delete endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools [T1685].
Medusa actors place tooling, such as Rclone, in pre-existing Windows Defender excluded folders for stealth. [T1564.012].
